claims.statement: Open-Inspect is designed for single-tenant deployment only: a shared GitHub App installation defines the access boundary, the system performs no per-user repository access validation at session creation, and user OAuth tokens exist for PR creation/attribution with fallback to the shared App bot for users without SCM tokens.

The documented deployment recommendations for the single-tenant model are operational controls: deploy behind the organization's SSO/VPN, install the GitHub App only on intended repositories (its installation scope is the system's access scope), and restrict sign-in via ALLOWED_USERS, ALLOWED_EMAILS, ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAINS, and ALLOWED_GITHUB_ORGS admission variables.

The system circulates six credential kinds — GitHub App installation tokens (brokered git auth), user OAuth tokens (PR creation and attribution), sandbox auth tokens (single-session sandbox→control-plane calls), WebSocket tokens (single-session client connections), managed LLM subscription tokens (OpenAI/xAI), and per-service sig1 signatures — and the README's token table records the four core rows.

Service-to-service authentication uses the sig1 signature format: each of the four services (web, slack-bot, github-bot, linear-bot) signs a canonical newline-delimited string (sig1, service, timestampMs, nonce, method, pathname, canonicalized query, body SHA-256 hex, actor) with its own secret, and the signature header is `sig1.<timestampMs>.<nonce>.<64-hex>` carrying X-OpenInspect-Service and optional X-OpenInspect-Actor headers.

The sig1 canonical request string layout and grammar are frozen by immutable golden vectors (test-fixtures/service-auth-vectors.json); any change to canonicalization requires a new format tag (sig2), not an edit to the vectors or buildCanonicalRequestString.
The sig1 query canonicalization decodes key=value entries, sorts them bytewise by key\0value, and re-encodes them, so ?a=1&b=2 and ?b=2&a=1 sign identically while a query and no query never collide.

Verification of a sig1 signature parses the header grammar and checks timestamp freshness (within TOKEN_VALIDITY_MS, 5 minutes) before the request body is buffered, so a malformed or stale header never costs a body read; only the HMAC comparison needs the body hash.

authenticate() resolves every non-public, non-sandbox request to a typed Principal at the edge: a verified sig1 channel yields a service principal, and a service:web request on a webService:"user" route additionally requires a Better Auth session that upgrades the principal to a user principal; requests with no recognized credential return failedScheme "none", which is the only scheme eligible for sandbox-token fallback routes.

Sandbox tokens are deliberately NOT verified by authenticate(): the router verifies them itself because it needs the session id from the path and a Durable Object round-trip, making the router the single place a sandbox principal is assembled.

The control plane holds one sig1 verification secret per service (SERVICE_AUTH_SECRET_WEB, SERVICE_AUTH_SECRET_SLACK_BOT, SERVICE_AUTH_SECRET_GITHUB_BOT, SERVICE_AUTH_SECRET_LINEAR_BOT); an absent secret is a 500 misconfiguration that blocks that service entirely rather than a 401 rejection, and a missing outbound secret is a hard error at call construction.

Sig1 request bodies are buffered under a hard cap (SERVICE_REQUEST_MAX_BODY_BYTES = 16 MiB, 413 over) because the signature covers the body hash; after verification the consumed body is rebuilt into a new Request so handlers still read it.

Sig1 nonce-reuse detection is best-effort and log-only: an in-isolate Map bounded to 5,000 entries whose entries expire with the signature validity window (TOKEN_VALIDITY_MS), with oldest-expiry eviction; it does not reject requests.

Actor assertions are namespace-restricted: ASSERTION_RIGHTS maps each bot to its own namespace (slack-bot→slack, github-bot→github, linear-bot→linear) and web to null (its identity arrives via token exchange, never assertion); a mismatched namespace is denied with 401, and a valid assertion is resolved against the D1 user_identities table to a canonical user id (null when never seen).

Better Auth runs inside the control plane as the user-authentication authority with the canonical SQL adapter: its user model IS the users table and its account model IS user_identities, so bot-created identities are natively signable accounts; sessions (auth_sessions, 7-day expiry, 24-hour updateAge) and OAuth state (auth_verifications with hashed identifiers) stay in Better Auth-owned tables, encryptOAuthTokens is enabled, and implicit account linking is deliberately enabled with users.email_verified as the linking gate.

Email verification is only written for attesting providers (Slack and Linear, EMAIL_ATTESTING_PROVIDERS) — the same weight as completed OAuth proof and what admits users through Better Auth's implicit-linking gate; every other provider's attribution stays unproven until sign-in proof mints it.

The Next.js web app is a framework-free BFF that holds no OAuth provider credentials or admission policy: it proxies an exact allowlist of Better Auth routes (BROWSER_AUTH_PROXY_ROUTES: sign-in/social, callback/github, callback/google, get-session, sign-out, error) through a sig1-signed forward carrying only the opaque session cookie and a trusted client IP header, so redirects and host-only cookies stay scoped to the web origin while Better Auth lives in the control plane.

Session validation for protected resources performs a non-refreshing Better Auth session read (disableRefresh: true) so resource requests never extend expiry or write D1; a malformed session or session.userId/user.id mismatch raises SessionIntegrityError which maps to 500, not a fallback or anonymous downgrade.

Identity enforcement is a single entry point (applyIdentityEnforcement) that owns reject → derive → requires-user in order: caller-supplied identity fields (userId, spawnSource, authProvider, authUserId, actorUserId, scmToken, scmRefreshToken, scmUserId for spawning routes; authorId for prompts; per-route subsets for ws-token and lifecycle) are rejected with 400 against the raw pre-Zod body because every schema is strip-mode; identity is derived only from the verified principal; and requires-user routes (session-create, ws-token, automation-create) fail closed with 403 when no participant can be derived.

deriveIdentity maps principals to identity: a user principal is its own canonical user with spawnSource "user"; the userless web service credential derives no participant; bot services derive their verified actor's participant id (ns:id format) and canonical id (possibly null) with the service name as spawnSource; sandbox principals derive null and are kept off identity routes by the router's allowlist (failing closed with 403 if that ever changes).

resolveCanonicalUserId creates the canonical user from the VERIFIED actor on first sight (body display fields only decorate), failing closed with 500 rather than writing anonymous attribution; it is shared by session-create and automation-create so the two routes cannot drift.

UserStore.resolveOrCreateUser is the canonical-resolution primitive: look up by (provider, providerUserId), refresh identity metadata and user display fields, backfill a missing email, re-link an identity to another user when that user owns the email (preventing permanent splits), link across providers by verified email, or create user+identity as a batch with one retry on the UNIQUE-constraint race.

When two canonical users are the same person, mergeUsers converges the loser's entire graph onto the survivor; it is deliberately a library plus operator CLI, never an HTTP endpoint (a merge primitive on an authenticated surface adds abuse surface for no safety gain), is dry-run by default, executes as one atomic batch ordered to satisfy every foreign key with explicit dedup rules, re-points auth_sessions rather than deleting them, backfills the survivor's email only when it has none, and is idempotent except one documented non-re-derivable window covered by a printed recovery record.

GitHub App brokering: the control plane (sole holder of GITHUB_APP_ID, GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY, GITHUB_APP_INSTALLATION_ID) generates a 10-minute RS256 JWT (iat back-dated 60s for clock skew) from the PKCS#8 private key, exchanges it at POST https://api.github.com/app/installations/:id/access_tokens for a ~1-hour installation token, and caches the token in per-isolate memory plus KV (github:installation-token:v1 keys) usable only while younger than 50 minutes AND holding ≥5 minutes remaining lifetime, with single-flight refreshes and non-fatal KV failures.

The GitHub App RSA private key must be PKCS#8 PEM (BEGIN PRIVATE KEY): importPrivateKey fails otherwise with an error instructing conversion via `openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -inform PEM -outform PEM -nocrypt -in key.pem -out key-pkcs8.pem` — the operational gotcha for operators.

Git auth for sandboxes is served on demand: generateCredentialHelperAuth returns username "x-access-token", the cached installation token, and its expiry (from getCachedInstallationTokenWithExpiry, so the sandbox credential helper can cache its copy until shortly before expiry); ScmCredentialsService wraps this, mapping permanent provider errors to 500 and transient ones to 502 and never logging the returned password.

User SCM OAuth tokens live in the user_scm_tokens D1 table keyed by provider_user_id with access token, refresh token, and expiry encrypted at rest using TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY; upsertTokens is monotonic (overwrites only when excluded.token_expires_at is newer, user_id COALESCEd) so a stale client token cannot clobber a server-side refresh, and casUpdateTokens rotates only if the stored refresh-token ciphertext still equals the expected value (cas_conflict otherwise); GitHub's missing expires_in falls back to an 8-hour default and freshness uses a 60-second buffer.

SCM credentials flow only through server-side enrichment, never caller bodies: on session-create the route resolves a credential authority and fills scmUserId/scmLogin/encrypted tokens server-side — browser sessions use the browser_session authority (accounts enumerated via the Better Auth API; the access token is fetched from Better Auth and re-encrypted with the control-plane key; Better Auth owns refresh-token storage so the long-lived refresh credential is never copied into a second store), while bot/service callers retain the legacy D1 UserScmTokenStore authority; a user principal missing browser-session provenance is a hard error, never a silent legacy fallback, and users without a linked GitHub account enrich nothing (App-bot PR fallback).

At PR creation time SessionPullRequestService re-resolves the repository target defensively (the sandbox caller is untrusted), pushes with a fresh App push-auth token, and creates the pull request with prAuth = input.promptingAuth ?? appAuth — the prompting user's OAuth token when available (attribution plus GitHub-enforced write access) and the shared App token otherwise (e.g. Linear-triggered sessions).

The sandbox auth token is a single-session bearer: reserveSpawnIdentity performs a two-phase write (phase 1 persists the new sandbox id with credentials invalidated; phase 2 publishes the SHA-256 token hash scoped to the reserved identity), the plaintext token (generateId() — 16 random bytes hex) exists only in memory and the provider launch payload, and rotating hash plus sandbox id on every respawn locks a stale bridge out exactly like a fresh spawn — including a fresh identity for the prebuilt-image restore retry since a failed provider create may have left a live orphan.

Sandbox token verification never happens locally: the router POSTs the presented Bearer token to the owning session DO (SessionInternalPaths.verifySandboxToken) and only on success sets the sandbox principal; a failed verification is 401 and an unreachable DO is 503 (could not be authenticated, not merely rejected). On user-or-service-with-sandbox-fallback routes the sandbox token is tried only when the sig1 attempt failed with failedScheme "none", so a recognized-but-invalid service credential is terminal.

The DO-side token verifier (isValidSandboxToken) prefers the stored auth_token_hash with a timing-safe compare, falling back to the plaintext auth_token column only for legacy rows; the DO rejects dead sandbox statuses with 410 but allows boot-time states because the git credential broker is already called during the initial clone before the WebSocket flips the row to ready, and handlers re-check sandbox id and credential hash after the non-storage token-hash await so a mid-flight respawn cannot authenticate against replaced credentials.

WebSocket clients authenticate by exchanging a short-lived WS token: POST /sessions/:id/ws-token (a requires-user identity-enforced route) forwards only the verified participant and display-only SCM fields; WsTokenHandler upserts the participant (accepting client-sent encrypted SCM tokens only when newer than the stored expiry, coalescing against server-side refreshes), generates a 32-byte hex token via generateId(32), stores only its SHA-256 hash plus ws_token_created_at, and returns the plaintext once; on subscribe the DO hashes the presented token, looks up by hash, and enforces a 24-hour TTL (WS_TOKEN_TTL_MS) with close codes 4001 (missing/invalid/expired) and 4003 (already subscribed).

Secrets live in three scopes (global, repository, environment) sharing one store plumbing layer (scoped-secrets.ts), one encryption key (REPO_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY), and one cap set; the session fold (buildSessionTargetSecretSources) orders sources lowest-precedence-first — global plus member repos in reverse position order (primary wins collisions) for repo/ad-hoc sessions, and global plus that environment's secrets ONLY for environment-launched sessions (member repos never contribute).

mergeSecretSources folds ordered sources case-insensitively (keys normalized to uppercase), reports per-source byte attribution and cross-source collisions, and computes total bytes against the combined cap; per scope the caps are 50 keys, 16 KB per value, 64 KB total values, and 128 KiB combined per session; duplicate keys after normalization (foo vs FOO) are rejected rather than last-wins.

A reserved-key list blocks user secrets from shadowing system environment variables — including SANDBOX_AUTH_TOKEN, CONTROL_PLANE_URL, GITHUB_APP_TOKEN, SESSION_CONFIG, SANDBOX_ID, PATH, and HOME — and keys must match [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]* up to 256 chars.

All secrets at rest are AES-256-GCM encrypted (encryptToken/decryptToken over Web Crypto: 96-bit random IV, base64(IV‖ciphertext)); this covers scoped secrets, user_scm_tokens, the commit-signing private key, and sandbox access values, and decryption failures raise SecretDecryptionError carrying the failing key but never plaintext or ciphertext.

Encryption-key management fails loud: env-validation.ts eagerly validates REPO_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY and TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY are present, strict base64, and decode to exactly 32 bytes (AES-256) — a malformed key would otherwise survive graph construction and throw mid-spawn, a short one would silently downgrade to AES-128/192 — and an unconfigured key means refusing to operate, never plaintext fallback; the commit-signing store likewise returns 503 without REPO_SECRETS_ENCRYPTION_KEY.

Secrets are injected as environment variables at spawn: the DO's UserEnvResolver decrypts contributing scopes, folds and audits the merge, and derives the managed-provider env (CONTROL_PLANE_OAUTH_KEYS like OPENAI_OAUTH_*/XAI_OAUTH_* are stripped from the exposed payload; in managed provider_account mode the provider's API-key variable is deleted and a *_OAUTH_MANAGED marker set so the in-sandbox CLI uses the control-plane broker); the payload rides CreateSandboxConfig.userEnvVars and refreshed only by a new spawn.

Provider launch env precedence protects the trust chain: system variables (SANDBOX_AUTH_TOKEN, CONTROL_PLANE_URL, SANDBOX_ID, timeout, repo fields) are applied after user values and therefore override them — a user-controlled secret cannot spoof the control-plane URL or token — and a reserved set of launch env vars (SESSION_CONFIG, VNC password, ports, snapshot markers) is stripped from user input entirely, as pinned by test_sandbox_env_vars.py.

Managed LLM subscription tokens (OpenAI ChatGPT, xAI SuperGrok) are stored in the scoped OAuth secret stores (global/repo/environment scopes) and refreshed by control-plane brokers, not sandboxes: the OpenAI token broker returns cached tokens until within a 5-minute refresh buffer and refreshes single-flight per isolate with D1 re-reads covering cross-isolate rotation; sandboxes call POST /sessions/:id/openai-token-refresh (or xai) with the sandbox token, and the route 409s unless the session's auth mode for that provider is legacy_scoped_oauth.

Provider-account credentials (connected ChatGPT/SuperGrok accounts) are encrypted with PROVIDER_ACCOUNTS_ENCRYPTION_KEY using AES-256-GCM with additional authenticated data binding each ciphertext to its version, provider account id, provider, and credential schema version, so ciphertexts cannot be transplanted between rows.

Commit signing is brokered and GitHub-only: the control plane holds a singleton OpenSSH Ed25519 private key (commit_signing_configuration row, private key AES-256-GCM encrypted alongside committer name/email, public key, and SHA256: fingerprint); PUT /commit-signing validates the key fully (unencrypted OpenSSH container only — none/none cipher/kdf, Ed25519 only, inner/outer public key consistency, padding verified, plus a sign/verify probe) and non-GitHub SCM deployments return an explicit enabled:false so sandboxes commit unsigned rather than failing the session.

The sandbox-side GitSigningRuntime applies signing per-repository with git config --local (gpg.format=ssh, gpg.ssh.program=<oi-git-sign path>, user.signingkey=key::<publicKey>, commit.gpgsign=true, author/committer identity), validating the fetched configuration as a strict pydantic discriminated union (extra=forbid; publicKey must match ssh-ed25519 <base64>); a disabled configuration runs --unset-all over the signing keys (tolerating exit codes 1/5) and sets a plain identity (prompt author or OpenInspect <open-inspect@noreply.github.com>), and a repository missing .git is a hard error.

There is a deliberate scope split between the two git config flows: the credential helper is installed once with git config --global (shim at /usr/local/bin/oi-git-credentials plus credential.useHttpPath=true), while signing config is per-repo --local so it can be reset per prompt without touching credential routing; the bridge initializes signing once before the first WebSocket connect (a non-retryable GitSigningError is fatal to the run loop) and refreshes before every prompt via _configure_git_identity with the prompt author.

oi-git-sign is a stateless ssh-keygen shim: non-sign invocations exec the stock ssh-keygen, while -Y sign reads the bounded payload (≤1 MiB) and the key:: literal public key (key material is never written to disk — pinned by test_initialize_fetches_public_configuration_without_creating_key_files), computes the SHA256 fingerprint, POSTs to /sessions/:id/commit-signing with the X-Open-Inspect-Signing-Fingerprint header and the sandbox token, validates the response armor strictly (≤16 KiB, SSHSIG magic), and writes it atomically; its error type carries no request, response, or credential bytes.

The control-plane signing endpoint enforces key continuity: it decrypts the stored key, rejects a fingerprint mismatch with 409 ("Commit signing key changed") so a stale-configured repository cannot obtain signatures from a rotated key, caps the payload at 1 MiB with 413, requires both the fingerprint header and non-empty payload, signs with SSHSIG v1 (git namespace, SHA-512 digest, Ed25519) and returns the armored signature no-store; interoperability with stock ssh-keygen -Y verify is pinned by a test asserting `Good "git" signature`.

The commit-signing Ed25519 key has its own import constraint: WebCrypto cannot import an OpenSSH private-key container, so the parser extracts the 32-byte seed and wraps it in a hand-built minimal PKCS#8 structure (ED25519_PKCS8_PREFIX + seed) before crypto.subtle.importKey("pkcs8", ...) — distinct from the GitHub App RSA key's PKCS#8 requirement, and encrypted OpenSSH keys are rejected outright; the fingerprint is SHA256 over the public key blob matching ssh-keygen -lf output.

The in-sandbox git credential helper implements git's credential protocol backed by the control plane: it mints fresh short-lived SCM credentials at POST {control_plane}/sessions/{session_id}/scm-credentials using the sandbox token, caches to /run/oi/scm-creds.json (mode 0600) with a 5-minute refresh buffer under an advisory lock, only authorizes requests whose protocol is https and whose host equals VCS_HOST (blocking exfiltration to attacker hosts via submodule URLs), and never falls back to the stale cache or serves store/erase actions.
